body:
Why INA officers faced trial

After Japan's defeat in the Second World War, many INA officers and soldiers came into British custody. The British authorities regarded Indian soldiers who had joined the INA as having fought against the Crown while previously owing allegiance to the British Indian Army.

The British therefore brought selected INA officers before military courts. These proceedings are commonly known as the INA trials or Red Fort trials, because the best-known court-martial was conducted at the Red Fort in Delhi.

The central issue was whether men who had fought against British forces as INA officers should be punished under military law, even though they claimed to have acted for India's independence.

The first major joint trial

The first major joint Red Fort court-martial opened on 5 November 1945. The 3 accused officers were:

  • Shah Nawaz Khan
  • Prem Kumar Sahgal, also spelled Sehgal
  • Gurbaksh Singh Dhillon

The officers were prosecuted for offences connected with taking up arms against the British Crown. Their public association with the INA, rather than the detailed legal arguments of the court-martial, became the principal focus of nationwide political attention.

The INA Defence Committee

The Congress helped organise legal support for INA prisoners. Leading lawyers participated in the defence. Bhulabhai Desai played an especially important role in presenting the defence case. Jawaharlal Nehru also joined the legal defence effort.

This involvement demonstrates an important distinction: Congress leaders had differed from Bose over political methods, but many strongly opposed the prosecution of INA personnel after the war. Support for the prisoners did not necessarily amount to endorsement of every wartime decision taken by the INA.

Why the trials provoked widespread protests

The trials brought the INA's activities to the attention of a much wider Indian public. Many people viewed the accused as nationalists who had fought for independence rather than as ordinary military offenders.

The first 3 accused were also widely presented as symbols of unity across religious communities. This strengthened the appeal of the campaign for their release.

Meetings, student demonstrations, processions and strikes took place in several parts of India. In Calcutta in November 1945, student demonstrations associated with opposition to the trials developed into broader public unrest. Workers and other groups joined the agitation.

Protests continued into February 1946, including renewed demonstrations in Calcutta over the punishment of another INA officer. The trials thus became a link between wartime armed resistance and post-war civilian mobilisation.

The verdict and remission of sentences

The 3 officers in the first joint trial were found guilty and received sentences that included transportation for life. However, the Commander-in-Chief, Claude Auchinleck, remitted these sentences on 4 January 1946. Their dismissal from military service and related penalties were not similarly cancelled.

Remission is not acquittal

The court-martial found the officers guilty. The subsequent remission meant that the principal sentences were not enforced. It did not mean that the court had acquitted them.

The decision reflected the difficult political situation created by the trials and widespread demands for the prisoners' release. The INA had not won its military campaign, but its treatment after the war generated sympathy that reached far beyond its surviving members.

Effect on the colonial government

The protests demonstrated the strength of public identification with the INA. They also raised concerns for British authorities about how continued prosecution might affect political order and the attitudes of Indian personnel serving in the colonial armed forces.

It would be inaccurate to say that every Indian soldier supported the INA or that the trials caused the British Indian Army to collapse. Their significance was that they exposed the political difficulty of relying indefinitely on Indian personnel to maintain colonial rule.

Prelims focus

  • 5 November 1945: First major joint INA court-martial opened at the Red Fort, Delhi.
  • Accused: Shah Nawaz Khan, Prem Kumar Sahgal and Gurbaksh Singh Dhillon.
  • Bhulabhai Desai: Leading defence lawyer in the INA trial.
  • Jawaharlal Nehru: Associated with the INA legal defence effort.
  • 4 January 1946: Commander-in-Chief Claude Auchinleck remitted the principal sentences of the 3 officers.
  • Trap: Remission of their sentences was not the same as acquittal by the court-martial.

[Sources: Indira Gandhi National Open University, History of India VIII (c. 1857–1950), Unit 19, 'Towards Independence: 1945–1947', section 19.4.1, printed pp. 271–272; Selected Works of Jawaharlal Nehru, First Series, vol. 14, p. 368, 'On the Release of the I.N.A. Officers', 5 January 1946, consulted through the Nehru Archive; Cambridge University Press, 'The Right to Wage War against Empire: Anticolonialism and the Challenge to International Law in the Indian National Army Trial of 1945', section on the first INA trial; online sources consulted 22 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: The first joint INA trial led to convictions, then remission of life sentences on 4 January 1946; public demonstrations continued into February.
pictures.caption: Trial, conviction, public response and remission.

title: The Red Fort INA Trials and the Nationalist Response, 1945–1946

body:
What was the Royal Indian Navy uprising?

The Royal Indian Navy (RIN) uprising of February 1946 was a revolt by Indian naval personnel against their working conditions and British naval authority. It is also called the Royal Indian Navy mutiny or the naval ratings' strike.

A rating is an enlisted member of a navy who is not a commissioned officer. Most of the protesters were Indian ratings serving under a naval organisation whose senior command was predominantly British.

Although the immediate grievances related to service conditions, the movement soon expressed broader nationalist demands. It therefore belonged both to the history of military discontent and to the late phase of India's freedom struggle.

The beginning at HMIS Talwar

The uprising began on 18 February 1946 at HMIS Talwar in Bombay, now Mumbai. The ratings protested against poor-quality food and other conditions of service.

HMIS Talwar was a Royal Indian Navy signals-training shore establishment. The name can be misleading: despite the naval designation, the protest began at a shore establishment, not on a warship sailing at sea.

Discontent had developed from several connected causes:

  • Poor food and living conditions: Ratings objected to the quality of meals and their general treatment.
  • Racial discrimination: Indian personnel resented unequal treatment and insulting behaviour by some British officers.
  • Pay and service inequalities: Differences between the treatment of Indian and European naval personnel contributed to resentment.
  • Nationalist influence: The INA trials and other anti-colonial developments encouraged ratings to connect their service grievances with the wider demand for independence.

These causes operated together. Describing the uprising as only a food protest ignores its political demands; describing it as a centrally planned national revolution ignores the importance of actual service grievances.

The strike committee and its demands

As the unrest spread, the ratings established a coordinating body commonly known as the Naval Central Strike Committee. M. S. Khan served as its president, and Madan Singh was associated with its leadership.

The demands combined improvements in naval service with nationalist objectives.

Service demandsPolitical demands
Better food and treatmentRelease of INA prisoners
More equal pay and conditions for Indian ratingsRelease of political prisoners
Removal of discriminatory practicesWithdrawal of Indian troops from Indo-China and Java

This distinction is useful because a question may classify the revolt as either a protest over service conditions or a nationalist uprising. It had elements of both.

Spread beyond Bombay

The action at HMIS Talwar encouraged ratings at other ships and shore establishments to join. The movement spread within Bombay and to other naval centres, including Karachi and Calcutta.

Accounts commonly used in government commemorations and teaching material describe participation by about 20,000 ratings, 78 ships and 20 shore establishments. These are approximate figures; historical studies do not all use identical totals or counting methods.

In Karachi, personnel associated with HMIS Hindustan became involved in the uprising. The spread demonstrated that the unrest was not confined to one kitchen, one ship or one isolated naval unit.

Flags and political solidarity

In some demonstrations, ratings displayed symbols associated with the Congress, the Muslim League and the Left. These actions expressed a desire for unity across political and religious divisions against colonial rule.

However, displaying these symbols did not mean that the Congress, the Muslim League and Communist organisations jointly directed the naval uprising. The position taken by their leaders became particularly important when the revolt approached its end.

Prelims focus

  • 18 February 1946: Beginning of the RIN uprising at HMIS Talwar, Bombay.
  • HMIS Talwar: Naval signals-training shore establishment.
  • M. S. Khan: President of the Naval Central Strike Committee.
  • Karachi: Important centre of the uprising, including HMIS Hindustan.
  • Commonly cited scale: About 20,000 ratings, 78 ships and 20 shore establishments.
  • Trap: The uprising began with service grievances but developed nationalist demands; it was not merely a dispute over food.

[Sources: UK Parliament, Hansard, House of Commons, 'Royal Indian Navy (Mutiny)', 22 February 1946, vol. 419, cols. 1441–1443; Indira Gandhi National Open University, History of India VIII (c. 1857–1950), Unit 19, section 19.4.1, printed pp. 272–273; Government of India, National War Memorial, 'Indian Navy', section on the 1946 RIN mutiny; sources consulted 22 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Naval ratings at a British-era dock establishment in Bombay, 1946.

title: The Royal Indian Navy Uprising of February 1946: Causes and Spread

body:
How a naval protest became a wider public crisis

The uprising did not remain confined to naval personnel. In Bombay, students, workers and members of the public expressed support for the ratings. Some provided food and other assistance, while political groups and labour organisations called for demonstrations and strikes.

This support was significant because it brought together a protest within the armed forces and civilian dissatisfaction with colonial rule. A conflict that had begun at a naval establishment now affected the streets, factories and transport activity of a major Indian city.

The Bombay general strike of 22 February 1946

On 22 February 1946, a major strike and public demonstrations took place in Bombay in support of the naval ratings. Communist organisations and sections of the labour movement played an important role in mobilising workers. Students and other civilians also participated.

Protests occurred in a tense atmosphere. Clashes developed between sections of the public and the colonial authorities, and police and military action resulted in deaths and injuries.

It is important to distinguish the naval ratings' strike from the civilian general strike. They were connected events, but they involved different participants: naval personnel in the first and workers and other members of the public in the second.

Congress and Muslim League responses

Senior leaders of the Indian National Congress and the All-India Muslim League did not formally lead the naval uprising. They expressed concern about the escalation of violence and urged the ratings to end their action.

Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel and Muhammad Ali Jinnah played important roles in persuading the ratings to surrender. The main uprising ended on 23 February 1946.

The appeals by Congress and League leaders must not be confused with an absence of nationalist sympathy for the grievances of Indian servicemen. The political leadership's immediate response to an armed-services revolt was different from the widespread support expressed for INA prisoners through legal defence and public agitation.

Why the revolt ended

The ratings faced the superior military resources of the colonial state and did not receive the broad support from other armed forces that would have been necessary to sustain a general military rebellion. Leading political organisations were also unwilling to endorse the continuation of the mutiny.

After the surrender, some ratings faced disciplinary consequences despite expectations that their grievances would receive fair consideration. The revolt ended without achieving the transfer of political power or a general collapse of British military command.

Historical significance

The uprising demonstrated that resentment against British rule could develop inside an important colonial armed service and connect with civilian anti-colonial protest. It increased uncertainty about the political reliability of Indian personnel and the cost of maintaining British authority.

At the same time, the revolt's suppression and surrender show why its significance must be stated carefully. The naval uprising was one major element of the late-colonial crisis, not a military victory that independently ended British rule.

Prelims focus

  • 22 February 1946: Major Bombay workers' strike and civilian demonstrations supported the naval ratings.
  • Communist and labour organisations: Important in mobilising civilian support.
  • Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel: Congress leader associated with appeals for the ratings to surrender.
  • Muhammad Ali Jinnah: Muslim League leader who also urged an end to the uprising.
  • 23 February 1946: The main naval uprising ended with the ratings' surrender.
  • Trap: Civilian support for the ratings did not mean the Congress and Muslim League officially directed the revolt.

[Sources: Indira Gandhi National Open University, History of India VIII (c. 1857–1950), Unit 19, 'Towards Independence: 1945–1947', section 19.4.1, printed pp. 273–274; UK Parliament, Hansard, House of Commons, 'India (Naval Mutiny and Civil Disturbances)', 26 February 1946, vol. 419, cols. 1750–1753; Jawaharlal Nehru, statement 'Unrest in the Navy', 24 February 1946, reproduced in the Nehru Archive; sources consulted 22 November 2026.]
